gap: No result ChatGPT got states that two named reviewers compared the Ulanzi tripods with the Peak Design Travel Tripod by hand: Ralph Mayhew pressed down on the top of both fully extended tripods and found the Peak Design legs bent 'significantly more' than the Zero Y's, and Dan Carr (Shutter Muse) put the Peak Design carbon at 1,307 g and the aluminum at 1,613 g on his scales (17 g and 53 g over Peak Design's 1.29 kg and 1.56 kg specs) and found the Ulanzi F38 'noticeably more stable than the Peak Design tripod at all heights'.
standout_why: I compared against the cited digitalnomads.world page (2026-10-17), which says 'We did not perform hands-on wind, vibration or overload tests' and gives only maker specs for the Zero Y and the Peak Design aluminum. The cited findingtheuniverse.com page has maker specs only and no Ulanzi. Pack Hacker gives weights without saying how it got them and has no Ulanzi or Befree. Fstoppers compared the Peak Design with an old Befree and a MeFoto and tested nothing. TechGearLab is in ChatGPT's results but not cited. It does have measured weights, stability scores and setup times for the Traveler 5C, Peak Design Travel and Befree Advanced, so those figures are not new. TechGearLab did not test any Ulanzi. Amateur Photographer, the cited page in both chats, returned HTTP 403, so I could not check it. Digital Camera World's guide came back truncated.
decides: This argues against ChatGPT's premium pick. Two named reviewers rate the Ulanzi tripods, at $280-320, as stiffer than the $400-600 Peak Design, so the Zero Y looks like the better value for stability and Peak Design's lead comes down to packed size (TechGearLab: 15.5 in folded). TechGearLab's stability score of 5.0/10 for the Sirui Traveler 5C, against 7.0 for the Peak Design and 7.4 for the Befree Advanced, already appears in a result ChatGPT got. It backs the 5C only for light setups. The Ulanzi evidence is a press-down test and a field judgement with no numbers, so it supports the pick but cannot settle it on its own.
